scheduling when the strong-smelling food is cooked / notification
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants used succinct, natural language and gave concrete reasons (health need, work calls, laundry). Example: Agent D: 'My doctor told me I have to eat it. For my heart.'
Repeated brief acknowledgements ('Okay, thanks.') appear many times (Rounds 9–11) without adding substance.
Speakers stayed consistent about physical constraints (shared kitchen, laundry in service yard) and did not confuse roles or facts.
evaluation.final_reason: Although a concrete, mutual arrangement was reached in Round 8 (Agent C asked D to avoid cooking on Monday/Wednesday/Friday evenings and D agreed: 'Okay. That works for me.'), Agent C reopened the issue in Round 12 saying weekdays are still a problem and proposing alternative days ('What about Tuesdays, Thursdays, or weekends?'). No new agreement followed Round 12, so the scheduling disagreement remains unresolved. Outstanding issues: (1) whether D will avoid cooking on Mon/Wed/Fri evenings (earlier acceptance was present but then questioned), and (2) how the timing interacts with laundry-hanging overnight — C seeks a different set of days but others' positions have not been re-accepted.
position_change_notes: Agent D moved from defensive (stating a medical need) to accommodating — agreeing to give warnings and to specific cook days ('Yeah, after 7 or on Saturdays is fine'; 'Okay. That works for me.').
Agent A shifted from proposing a ban to accepting time-based compromises (from 'nobody cook strong-smelling food' to suggesting after 7 p.m. or Saturdays).

Agent C initially raised the laundry concern, accepted a proposed schedule in Round 8 ('Okay, thanks.'), then later clarified that weekdays remain problematic and proposed different days in Round 12, indicating their earlier acceptance was conditional or based on an assumption that later changed.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A asked that nobody cook strong-smelling food in the flat ('Just to explain...the smell is a problem'); Agent B confirmed it's a problem for them (room next to kitchen). This expresses a demand that conflicts with existing cooking practice but no one responsible has replied yet.

Agent C added that their laundry picks up smells. Agent D responded with a medical need ('My doctor told me I have to eat it. For my heart.'), creating a clear incompatibility between D's need to cook and others' desire to avoid smells.

Agent A accepted D's health reason ('If it's for your health, I get it') and shifted to seeking a management solution; Agent D asked when would be better to cook. The direct confrontation eased into problem-solving but the core incompatibility remains open.

Agent A proposed specific preferred times ('any time after that would be better. Or on Saturdays'); Agent B offered a mitigation (warning so they can close door). This reduced tenor of disagreement to scheduling details.
Agent D agreed to give a warning ('Okay, I can do that.'); Agent A asked whether after 7 p.m. or Saturday would work. No new opposing position introduced, but not all constraints addressed yet.

Agent D agreed to the suggested timing ('Yeah, after 7 or on Saturdays is fine') and Agent A accepted. This is a concrete mutual scheduling arrangement between some parties but C's laundry timetable has not been resolved yet.

Agent C pointed out that time doesn't solve their laundry problem ('the time doesn't really matter for the laundry. It's still out there drying in the evening'), reopening the incompatibility the earlier agreement left unaddressed.

Agent C proposed specific laundry-aware days ('I do my laundry on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday evenings. Could you cook it on the other days?') and Agent D explicitly agreed ('Okay. That works for me.'). This produced a concrete, mutual spoken arrangement resolving the immediate scheduling conflict among the parties who spoke.
Only acknowledgements ('Okay, thanks.') were exchanged; no substantive disagreement appeared.

Continuation of acknowledgements from Agent C ('Okay, thanks.') and no substantive dispute introduced.

Agent C stated weekdays remain a problem because laundry hangs all night and proposed alternative days ('What about Tuesdays, Thursdays, or weekends?'), which conflicts with the earlier spoken arrangement and reintroduces unresolved scheduling incompatibility.

substantive_insights: Conflict framed as nuisance vs. medical necessity: D's health need competes with others' desire to avoid smells.

Scheduling is the viable trade-off space; multiple constraints (work calls, laundry drying schedule, evenings when people are home) create combinatorial restrictions that make a simple schedule fragile.

A one-off mutual agreement can appear to resolve an issue in a speech-only setting, but if an affected party later clarifies an overlooked constraint (laundry overnight), the agreement can be reopened.
